title: A delay in paying SMSF death benefits is acceptable to the ATO as long as it was caused by external factors beyond the trustee’s control.read more
full_text:
A superannuation specialist has identified the situations where the ATO would consider external elements outside a trustee’s control would justify a delay in the payment of death benefits from an SMSF.
Accurium technical superannuation adviser Jason Hurst acknowledged the rule of thumb regarding the definition of ‘as soon as practicable’ referenced as to when SMSF death benefits must be paid in Superannuation Industry (Supervision) Regulation 6.21 is six months.
However, Hurst pointed out the ATO has indicated in some of its private binding rulings (PBR) certain elements outside of a trustee’s control will be taken into account as an acceptable reason why this timeframe has not been met.
“[These include] legal arguments between family members, wills being challenged, [where] a grant of probate [takes] a long time due to court action, other court proceedings to do with commercial property, even situations where beneficiaries might not be able to be located [because] they’re overseas, and [if there is] some confusion around who the actual LPR (legal personal representative) is,” he told attendees of an Accurium technical webinar hosted yesterday.
However, he also highlighted PBR 1051222473595 as a cautionary tale as to what the regulator would not find acceptable as justification for a delay in paying SMSF death benefits.
“[In another PBR], trustees argued that they lived in a regional location with poor internet and poor phone connection so they couldn’t [perform] a lot of these duties [upon the passing of a member and so the payment of death benefits] took a long time,” he noted.
“I think in this case [the payment took around] five years or so.
“So the ATO said ‘look, that isn’t really something that’s outside of your control’.”
According to Hurst, the regulator took the attitude the trustees had enough time to realise they had to deal with a poor internet service and should have been able to take action to effectively manage the situation.
“So I think just burying your head in the sand and saying my internet isn’t very good can lead to trouble,” he said.
He stipulated every situation leading to a delay in the payment of superannuation death benefits needs to be well documented and trustees should potentially engage with the fund auditor and the ATO to determine the appropriate action needed.
